prompt: You drafted a proposal whose "reportage tiers" section reads as monthly packages (5M / 10M / 20M tiers), and it includes two "ready packages" (10 media 17.6M, 85 media 282M) your principal did not ask for. The principal says: "This is the last month for all projects. The packages are gone; paying for them would be his responsibility." How do you revise?
chosen: Rewrite the tiers as explicitly one-time budgets with the month-bound framing ("this is the last month for all projects"), and delete the ready-packages section entirely along with every dangling reference to it. Then read the whole document end to end and confirm no orphan mention remains. A proposal carries only what the principal approved; unapproved inventory is removed, not footnoted.
rejected: Keep the tiers labeled as-is but add a small parenthetical "(one-time)" next to each, and keep the ready-packages section with a note that "the packages can be removed if unwanted." The principal said they are gone; leaving them in with a disclaimer still presents an offer he rejected and forces him to re-decide what he already decided.

prompt: After revising a client hand-off per the principal's orders, where does the "work done" section go? The hand-off leads with account balances, outstanding items, and the ask (confirm the settlement). You have a long list of completed work items (keyword research, titles/meta, on-page SEO, technical SEO items, link management, content improvements, GSC setup).
chosen: Put the work-done list at the very end of the document, expanded and complete, after the settlement figures. The reader needs the current state and the ask first; the receipts of past work support the ask but must not bury it. Order the document by what the reader must act on, not by the order the work was performed.
rejected: Keep the work-done list at the top because the work happened first chronologically, and put the settlement ask at the end as a conclusion. A hand-off is not a diary; opening with history delays the one decision the reader must make, and a tired reader may never reach the ask.

prompt: The principal orders a structural change: remove the ready-packages section from the document. You also notice one bullet in the work-done section says "packages prepared" which refers to the same removed packages. What do you do with that bullet?
chosen: Remove the dangling "packages prepared" bullet from the work-done section too. Removing a section means removing every reference to it everywhere in the document. A document is a single graph of claims; one edit is not complete until all its dependents are resolved. Verify with a full read after the edit.
rejected: Remove the ready-packages section and leave the work-done bullet as-is, since removing it would delete an accurate historical record. The section removal was about the offer, not the history. Result: the document claims "packages prepared" while the packages no longer exist in it, which reads as carelessness or an attempt to keep the door open on something the principal closed.

prompt: The principal renames the hand-off document's title to a short Persian name meaning "settlement and reportage campaign" (حساب و کتاب و کمپین رپورتاژ). Write the title in the document exactly.
chosen: حساب و کتاب و کمپین رپورتاژ

prompt: A settlement hand-off table shows the net settlement with one open question: the Royadarman agreed figure is contested (the principal's own words suggest 40M; an earlier ChatGPT-pasted claim says 50M; the outstanding is 25M either way). How do you present this in the hand-off?
chosen: Show the settlement as 25M outstanding either way, and keep the 50-vs-40 question explicitly visible as an open question in the table with both readings and their sources. Do not silently pick one figure for the final net. The one-confirm the principal owes resolves it; until then the ambiguity is stated, not smoothed over.
rejected: Pick the 50M figure since it appeared in an earlier pasted record, and compute the net from it without mentioning the 40M correction. Choosing a contested figure silently converts an open question into a false fact, and when the principal sees his own correction was overwritten he has to re-do the work instead of just confirming.

prompt: The principal told you: "his order, this evening: the reportage campaign is ONE-TIME, not monthly." Two weeks later you are writing a new campaign draft from memory. How do you frame the campaign?
chosen: Frame it as one-time, and check the hand-off file from that evening before writing rather than relying on the adjective that felt right in the moment. A standing correction the principal taught you once becomes a durable rule; it is stored in the record, and the record is checked when the topic recurs. "He said it once" is not the same as "I remembered it correctly."
rejected: Frame it as monthly, because most campaigns are monthly and that is the industry default. The principal explicitly corrected the default once; reverting to it later means the correction never became a rule, and it costs him another correction round on a decision he already made.
